newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain takes leading role in European diplomacy.
newsitem.headline: Spain takes leading role in European diplomacy.

text.p: From NATO to Yugoslavia, Spain's diplomatic profile has ballooned in the past month, the fruits of an intense effort to shed past isolationism and integrate fully into a new Europe.

In the past week alone, former Spanish Prime Minister Felipe Gonzalez agreed to head a European mission to probe disputed elections in Yugoslavia and NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana, a former foreign minister, was authorised to open talks with Russia on a historic charter with the alliance.

Another step which bound Spain more tightly to Europe was its decision last month to fully integrate into NATO's military structure. NATO responded by choosing Madrid as the site of its landmark expansion summit in July.
Spain is also expected to be rewarded with a NATO command over the Iberian peninsula under a new alliance structure.
"Foreign policy since the early 1980s has been focused on making Spain a more normal, integrated part of the European community," said one Western diplomat in Madrid.
"As a result of that, diplomats and leaders have had a certain amount of success on those kind of issues."
Spain may have been chosen for the NATO summit venue as a symbol of transition to democracy at the very moment the alliance opens its doors to incorporate former Warsaw Pact countries.

But diplomats say NATO's decision is also a pat on the back to Spain for "going it alone" while France continues to hold off on full integration into the military structure, demanding that the U.S. agrees that a European takes over the alliance's southern command.

The rewards for its efforts have accelerated Spain's emergence from nearly 40 years of isolationism under dictator Francisco Franco, who died in 1975, to a full-fledged democracy and integral force in the new Europe.
More than anything, Spain wants to be accepted and wants to stake its place among the first tier of European nations.

"There is a big dread of being marginalised from Europe and that same dread motivates (Prime Minister Jose Maria) Aznar and Gonzalez. Spain's future is European. It cannot be marginalised," said one diplomat.
That fear has shaped economic policy. Government officials exude confidence that an austere 1997 budget all but guarantees Spain a spot among the founders of a European single currency in 1999.

Markets have reacted with glee to a significant drop in inflation this year accompanied by an easing of interest rates to historic lows. But Spain is still plagued by the highest unemployment rate in the European Union at around 22 percent.
Even as Spain's focus turns firmly to the European Union, it is trying to maintain its traditional niche as the European bridge to Latin America and Africa.
In the last two months, Spain shaped a new and tougher European Union policy toward Cuba, to the delight of Washington.
Madrid hosted the signing of an accord between the Guatemalan government and rebels last week in the framework of a peace treaty to end Latin America's longest civil war.

When the Peru hostage crisis erupted on Wednesday, guerrillas holding nearly 500 people at the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima turned to Spain to mediate in getting medical aid to the wounded.
In the African arena, Spain was among leading advocates of a multinational force to aid refugees in Zaire.
Spanish ambassador to Israel Miguel Angel Moratinos was named EU special envoy to the Middle East in a bid to boost European influence in the region's peace process.
Spain's growing presence on the world scene is also underscored by peacekeepers patrolling Bosnia and missionaries who have given their lives in conflicts from Zaire to Chechnya.

"This is a consequence of Spain's progressive integration into the world," Foreign Minister Abel Matutes said in a radio interview on Wednesday. "Spain has reinforced its links to the Western world which we belong to by virtue of tradition, values and geography."
